# State Policies Could Impede New Efforts to Increase Access to Medications for Opioid Use Disorder

**Authors:** Benjamin A. Barsky; Ateev Mehrotra; Haiden A. Huskamp

**Affiliations:** Interfaculty Initiative in Health Policy, Harvard University (BAB); Edmond & Lily Safra Center for Ethics, Harvard University (BAB); Department of Health Care Policy, Harvard Medical School (AM, HAH); Division of General Medicine, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (AM); OptumLabs Visiting Fellow (AM), Eden Prairie, MN.

After long delays and much advocacy, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) appears finally poised to create a special registration pathway that would facilitate the prescription of medications for opioid use disorder (MOUD) via telemedicine. Clinicians and policymakers who have pushed for this change will no doubt celebrate. The hope is that this change in federal policy will increase access to MOUD. But many are unaware that a large subset of Americans will be unable to get MOUD via telemedicine because of restrictive state policies.

## Policy Context

The Ryan Haight Online Pharmacy Consumer Protection Act of 2008 (Ryan Haight Act) requires that clinicians conduct an in-person medical evaluation before prescribing controlled substances, including buprenorphine, an evidence-based treatment for OUD. Given the potential for telemedicine to expand access to treatment, Congress passed subsequent legislation requiring the DEA to create a special registration pathway for clinicians to prescribe MOUD via telemedicine by 2019. This pathway was delayed, and clinicians and members of Congress have since pushed the DEA on their timetable on implementation.1,2

The DEA’s delay became moot at the start of the pandemic when federal regulators temporarily waived enforcement of the in-person rule for some controlled substances including buprenorphine. Their aim was to decrease COVID-19 transmission and increase MOUD access. Clinicians quickly responded to the waiver. Of all patients starting buprenorphine during the pandemic, 14-15% were via telemedicine.3,4 But when the public health emergency ends, so too will the waiver—reinstalling the in-person requirement as a barrier for access to treatment.

The DEA recently issued a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking signaling intention to begin the regulatory process necessary for the special registration pathway to become implemented and available for clinicians.5 (Note that other proposed federal regulatory reforms are occurring in parallel to the DEA’s special registration pathway for OUD treatment via telemedicine in Opioid Treatment Programs.6)

## How State Policies Will Become an Impediment

Although the special registration pathway’s exact parameters remain unclear, the expectation is that it will enable clinicians to prescribe MOUD without a preliminary in-person medical evaluation in at least some circumstances. What is underappreciated is how any such pathway can conflict with policies in many states that prevent clinicians from starting patients on MOUD via telemedicine. The state policies fall into two groups.

First, many states implemented legislation or policies before the public health emergency that restrict telemedicine use for MOUD prescribing. Generally, these laws and policies aim to decrease the risk of diversion, although no conclusive evidence currently supports that telemedicine use increases this risk. In New York, Indiana, Minnesota, and other states, clinicians cannot prescribe controlled substances to any patient without conducting an initial face-to-face medical evaluation. In states like Texas and Michigan, pharmacies have the authority to refuse dispensing prescription drugs based on the distance between a patient and their prescribing clinician. Such pharmacy-level barriers can be triggered when a patient sees via telemedicine a clinician physically located far from them. And in at least one state, Utah, prescribing controlled substances in telemedicine follow-up visits is prohibited even if it occurs after an initial in-person visit.

During the public health emergency, most states relaxed these restrictions to allow patients to start MOUD treatment via telemedicine. But these policy changes were temporary and, without new legislation or policies in these states, these policies will come back into effect and patients will have limited access to treatment via telemedicine. Although changing executive orders may be relatively easier, states with legislation limiting the use of MOUD via telemedicine will require amendments or new law.

Second, during the public health emergency, 8 states—Arkansas, Florida, Louisiana, New Hampshire, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, and South Carolina—imposed new restrictions in response to the DEA’s temporary waiver of the in-person rule. In doing so, these states—which comprise 16% of the US population—created conditions that made MOUD prescribing via telemedicine harder.

These restrictions come in many flavors. For example, in Arkansas, Governor Asa Hutchinson issued an executive order in March 2020, waiving a statutory provision that requires an in-person encounter before the establishment of any clinician-physician relationship. But he limited the waiver to the diagnosis and treatment of patients who do not require controlled substance prescriptions. As a result, clinicians in Arkansas have had to see patients in person before prescribing MOUD via telemedicine throughout the pandemic. In South Carolina, the medical licensing board issued a temporary rule in March 2020 approving the initiation of MOUD treatment via telemedicine without a preliminary in-person encounter. But that rule came with a requirement that clinicians evaluate patients in person within 60 days after termination of the public health emergency. The medical licensing board eventually rescinded this temporary rule in June 2021. Now, any patient prescribed with MOUD via telemedicine must undergo an initial in-person visit.

The DEA special registration pathway may prompt other states to issue similar policies. After all, states have the authority to regulate the practice of medicine. Under this constitutionally protected authority, they can decide who can prescribe controlled substances, and under what clinical circumstances they can do so. Thus, states can criminalize clinicians who prescribe MOUD without an initial in-person encounter or discipline them through civil or administrative means (e.g., medical license probation or removal). Considering that 8 states limited telemedicine use for OUD treatment at a moment of crisis—when in-person services became largely inaccessible due to COVID-19—we would not be surprised if some states decide to implement policies making implementation of the special registration pathway more difficult.

## Policy Changes Needed to Enable All Americans to Receive MOUD via Telemedicine

More than 200,000 people in the United States have died from drug overdoses in the last two years, with disproportionate mortality occurring among people of color, especially Black and American Indian or Alaska Native people.7,8 The best treatment available is MOUD.9 Telemedicine may increase access to and utilization of that treatment, improve MOUD treatment retention, and decrease overdose rates.10 This result could have important health equity implications given persistent deficiencies in MOUD availability in communities of color and rural areas. At the same time, achieving this result will require efforts and commitments to address the digital divide in telemedicine access.

The implementation of the special registration pathway by the DEA will be a critical step in terms of increasing access to MOUD via telemedicine, especially if it grants clinicians the same prescribing flexibility as they had during the public health emergency. But it is only the first step. Even with this new pathway, a large fraction of Americans will be unable to access MOUD in office-based settings via telemedicine.

The focus now turns to the states. If they want to increase access to OUD treatment, states with restrictions will have to remove legislation or change policies that restrict MOUD access via telemedicine. States could also enact legislation authorizing the prescribing of MOUD via telemedicine to the fullest extent permitted under federal law. This type of alignment between federal and state policy will help ensure access to evidence-based and life-saving treatment at a moment of historic need.
